# Cold Frame

## Overview

A glazed box on the ground, low to the south, is the cheapest way I know to buy six weeks at each end of the season. It is one of those bits of kit that pays for itself in a single spring: sown salads in February instead of April, and lettuces cut until the end of November without a heating bill attached to them. Mine sits against the south wall of the shed where it catches the low winter sun. It is not a greenhouse and I do not expect it to behave like one. It warms what is inside by day and holds some of that warmth into the night, and that is enough to push tender seedlings through the last frost. Everything below is what I did to build it and what has worked since. It cost me a morning and the price of a sheet of twinwall, and it has outlasted two of my seed trays. If I had to give up every other structure on the plot and keep one, this is the one I would keep, because it works hard for eight months of the year and asks for nothing but a wipe and a new lining each autumn.

## Setup

The box I built measures 60 by 120 cm and stands about 30 cm high at the low edge, with the glazed panels tilted at roughly 45 degrees so the face looks south and catches as much of the low sun as the plate can hold. The base is scrap timber I had left from a shelf job, screwed into a rectangle and set straight onto the soil, no foundations and nothing dug in. I laid a bed of sand inside, about 5 cm deep, levelled it with a batten pulled across, and set my pots and seed trays on that. The sand holds water and gives a steady footing, so the pots do not tip when I slide the lid over. The inside of the panels is lined with bubble wrap, tacked along the top and left hanging loose at the bottom, which halves the heat loss on a clear night. The hinged lid is the whole south face, on two small strap hinges at the ridge, and I prop it open with a cut batten once the air inside passes 20 C on a sunny morning. That prop is the only moving part and it lives hooked to the side of the base so I can find it. I check the lid opens and closes freely before I plant anything, because a lid that jams on a hot afternoon will cook the lot. The whole thing sits on a levelled strip of bare soil rather than paving, so any water that drains through the pots soaks away instead of pooling inside. I set it on two short runners of timber so the base does not sit flat on the wet ground, and the gap underneath keeps the bottom edge from rotting. It is light enough that I could lift it with one hand, which matters when I want to move it out of the way for the summer.

## Planting

Lettuce goes in first, a short row of a hardy butterhead, sown direct in February and thinned to 20 cm. Radish fills the gaps between the rows, pulled young at three or four weeks while the lettuce is still finding its feet. Spring onions go in as sets in the sand bed and stand right through until May, and I pull them as I need them rather than lifting the lot. Through the dark months I keep a tray of cut-and-come-again salad on the go, sowing a fresh pinch about every three weeks so there is always a leaf to pick, and I sow it thinly because a crowded tray of seedlings damps off in still air. The succession matters more than any single sowing: small and often beats one big row that bolts before I can eat it. When one sowing has been cut out I tip the spent compost onto the bed outside, refill the tray and sow again in the same spot, so the sand bed is never empty for more than a week. From April I start using it to harden off the tomatoes and the courgettes before they go out, taking the lid off in the day and closing it at night for a fortnight. In June it goes empty, and I lift the whole thing onto the path and use it as a carrot fly barrier over a short row instead.

## Maintenance

The panels get a wipe with a damp cloth whenever they cloud over with condensation, which is most weeks in winter. I use plain water and no detergent, since a film of soap on the inside catches the light and cuts the sun a little. The bubble wrap is renewed each autumn, since it goes brittle and tears where the sun hits it, and this is the one job I do not skip: a winter with ragged lining costs about two degrees on a clear night and the lettuce notices. The hinge screws get a turn in late winter when the timber has moved, and I check the lid has not dropped on one side, because a lid that sits crooked leaves a running gap along the top edge. In wind I weigh the lid down with a brick on the top edge so a gust does not flip it back on the hinge. The timber base gets a look each spring for rot along the bottom edge, and I have not had to replace a board yet.

## Notes

Slugs collect under the panels and along the timber base, so I lift the pots and look underneath every week or so, and a beer trap or two at the shaded end deals with the worst of them. Damping off is the other problem, and it comes from wet seed and still air, so I water sparingly at the root and open the lid on mild days to move the air through. The sand bed should be damp, never soaked. On a bright day in March the air inside can pass 25 C by eleven in the morning and drop to 2 C by midnight, so the lid has to be worked morning and evening rather than left alone. I keep a plastic bottle of water standing inside to take the chill off before it goes on the seedlings.
